claims.text: A nanoscale tungsten interfacial layer can create controlled interface coherency in HEA multilayers.
Tungsten-modified interface coherency can produce a transition from diffusion-mediated creep at lower temperatures to dislocation-mediated creep at higher temperatures.
The initial HEA multilayer coatings have coherent interfaces between their layers.
The proposed intervention is to introduce nanoscale tungsten transition layers at interfaces between HEA layers.
The low-temperature, low-stress testing region corresponds to diffusion-mediated creep, while the high-temperature, high-stress region corresponds to dislocation-mediated creep.
A tungsten layer adjusts the lattice mismatch between HEA layers and thereby modifies interface coherency.
Tungsten has a high melting point.
The atomic size of tungsten contributes to stabilization of coherent HEA interfaces.
A tungsten interlayer stabilizes coherent interfaces at lower temperatures.
Stabilized coherent interfaces limit dislocation nucleation.
Limiting dislocation nucleation favors diffusion-mediated creep.
Increasing temperature and stress thermally reduces the coherency of tungsten-modified interfaces.
Reduced interface coherency facilitates dislocation motion and causes a transition to dislocation-mediated creep.
Compared with HEA multilayers lacking tungsten interlayers, tungsten-modified multilayers will have a lower creep rate in the diffusion-controlled regime.
At higher temperatures, tungsten-modified multilayers will show a pronounced switch to dislocation activity detectable through dislocation density and creep strain-rate measurements.
HEA multilayers without engineered tungsten transition layers have a less distinct or uncontrolled creep-mechanism transition.
The effectiveness of a tungsten transition layer depends on its thickness and on the specific HEA composition.
An excessively thick tungsten layer or testing outside the targeted temperature and stress range may prevent the expected creep-mechanism transition.
